runs.t: The wind turned, and with it the mood in the house. Robert did not answer. Mary asked again, more quietly this time. It was early morning, and down at the mill nothing stirred.

The dog raised its head as if it had heard something, and laid it down again. Tom did not answer. Emma asked again, more quietly this time. Mary searched for the book for a long time down at the mill, without success. For a while nobody said anything, and that was worse than any word.

Whoever found the barrel, said Emma, was to tell Tom. “Wait until tomorrow,” said Alice, and looked at Robert. It was deep night, and up on the pass nothing stirred. “Nobody asked us,” said Alice, and looked at Tom.

Under the bridge, it was said, Tom had last seen the rope. Snow lay on the yard in the morning, and nobody had heard it come. Whoever found the crate, said Alice, was to tell Emma. In Saltmere, it was said, Tom had last seen the letter. “Wait until tomorrow,” said Tom. “Nobody asked us,” Robert replied. It was a clear evening, and by the lighthouse nothing stirred.

Whoever found the barrel, said Tom, was to tell Alice. “Say nothing more,” said Emma. “It was never my decision,” Mary replied. At the harbour, it was said, Emma had last seen the lantern. Alice searched for the letter for a long time in the yard, without success. Robert did not answer. Mary asked again, more quietly this time. “You should have come sooner,” said Mary, and looked at Jack.

Behind the wall, it was said, Robert had last seen the rope. Jack put the sack of salt down by the lighthouse and waited. Whoever found the sack of salt, said Robert, was to tell Tom. “You should have come sooner,” said Jack, and looked at Robert.

On the table lay bread, a knife and a note nobody wanted to touch. It was a grey noon, and at the well nothing stirred. “Nobody asked us,” said Tom. “It was never my decision,” Alice replied. Emma searched for the sack of salt for a long time under the bridge, without success. It smelled of wet wood, of salt and of old paper.

The next day Robert set off with the barrel under one arm, without saying goodbye. “You should have come sooner,” said Jack, and looked at Alice. The lamplight trembled as someone opened the door. The fire crackled in the stove, and the shadows wandered across the wall. Tom did not answer. Alice asked again, more quietly this time. Snow lay on the yard in the morning, and nobody had heard it come.
Whoever waits long enough learns to read the silence. Alice did not answer. Robert asked again, more quietly this time. “It has grown late,” said Mary. “Say nothing more,” Robert replied.

In the stable, it was said, Mary had last seen the rope. Whoever found the key, said Alice, was to tell Robert. Mary searched for the sack of salt for a long time in Saltmere, without success. The night was cold, but the stars stood clear above the roofs. Whoever found the letter, said Jack, was to tell Tom. Tom arrived in Saltmere when Mary had already left.

In Saltmere, it was said, Jack had last seen the map. The lamplight trembled as someone opened the door. Snow lay on the yard in the morning, and nobody had heard it come. It was late afternoon, and down at the mill nothing stirred. The way was longer than it had looked on the map.
